summary: Learners aged 9–11 learn to name, locate and characterise Earth's climate zones (tropical, temperate, polar, arid/desert, mountain), explain that latitude plus altitude and geography set which zone a place belongs to, and link each zone's climate to its characteristic ecosystems and ways of life. Two targeted surprises — a cold desert and a freezing peak on the Equator — confront the 'desert = hot' and 'latitude is everything' misconceptions. A banded map/globe makes the Equator→poles pattern visible; drag-the-latitude sorting and matching tasks add active causal reasoning and assessment.
misconceptions: All deserts are hot — 'desert' means dry; cold/polar deserts exist
Climate zones depend only on latitude — altitude and geography also set them (a tropical mountain can be cold)
Zone boundaries are sharp lines rather than gradual transitions
Temperate = boring/mild everywhere — temperate zones have strong seasons
A zone's plants/animals are there by chance rather than adapted to its climate

activities.title: Banded climate-zone atlas
steps: Study a world map (or globe) split into coloured latitude bands — tropical hugging the Equator, temperate mid-latitudes, polar caps near the poles — and name each band.
Reveal each band's climate profile (e.g. hot-and-wet, moderate-with-seasons, freezing) and its characteristic plants, animals and ways of life.
Drill down from a band into a biome scene — steaming rainforest, baking desert, frozen tundra — and describe how the zone's climate shapes what lives there.
Sweep attention from the Equator to the pole and describe how the ecosystems transform in step with the climate.
Examine two deliberately placed surprises: a COLD desert (dry but not hot) and a freezing mountaintop sitting right on the Equator; explain why each breaks a simple rule.
Combine more than one source (banded map + climate data + biome images) to describe a chosen zone.
activities.insight: Climate zones are a readable global pattern, not a list to memorise: climate (set mainly by latitude, modified by altitude and geography) shapes the ecosystems and human life found in each zone.

activities.title: Drag the latitude and altitude — watch the zone change
steps: Move a marker to different latitudes and predict, then check, which climate zone results.
Add an altitude slider: raise the marker on a tropical latitude and observe the zone shift toward cold/alpine, discovering that height can override latitude.
Sort animals, plants and types of home into the zone where they belong, and justify each placement by the zone's climate.
Build a case that shows latitude alone is not enough (e.g. a tropical peak that is freezing because of its altitude).
activities.insight: Latitude is the main control on a place's climate zone, but altitude can move a place into a colder zone, and geography (such as distance from the sea or mountains blocking rain) can make a place drier or give it more extreme seasons — so two places at the same latitude need not share a zone.

activities.title: Why is the Equator hot? — the angle-of-sunlight investigation
steps: Discuss the prompt: 'The Equator is hot all year and the poles are freezing. Some say the Equator is hottest because it is the part of Earth closest to the Sun. Is that why?'

Shine a torch straight down onto a globe near the Equator, then shine the same torch at a slant near a pole while keeping it at the same distance from the surface, and compare how large an area the light spreads over.
Explain in your own words why slanted rays spread the same heat over a larger area and so warm it less.
Apply the ideas to the Equatorial snowy mountain: explain how a place on the Equator — where rays are near-vertical and the lowlands are hot — can still be freezing at its summit because of altitude.
Answer: why are the tropics hot ALL year while many temperate places have cold winters?
activities.insight: A place's climate zone is decided mainly by latitude through the ANGLE at which sunlight strikes — near the Equator rays hit almost straight down and concentrate heat on a small area, while near the poles they strike at a slant and spread over a larger area, so it is colder. The Equator is not meaningfully closer to the Sun. Altitude and distance from the sea are additional controls; altitude is why a peak on the Equator can be freezing even though its lowlands are hot.

activities.title: Zone-matching and latitude-sequence check
steps: Match each zone to its description and to its characteristic plants, animals and ways of life.
Sequence a set of places by latitude from Equator to pole and predict each one's zone.
Answer multiple-choice items on 'what determines this zone?', including an item that describes a cold place near the Equator — decide what makes it cold.
Explain at least one example of how a climate zone affects the plants, animals or people living there.
activities.insight: Learners can independently name and describe the zones, state what determines each, and reason about exceptions such as a cold place near the Equator.

activities.title: Voices from contrasting zones
steps: Read or listen to short first-person accounts from people (or wildlife descriptions) living in contrasting zones — e.g. a rainforest, a cold tundra, a hot-dry desert.
Ask and answer questions about how the zone's climate changes daily life, food, shelter, or how plants and animals survive.
Compare two accounts and explain which climate features drive the differences.
activities.insight: A zone's plants, animals and people are shaped by (adapted to) its climate, not there by chance — the climate→life link made human and concrete.

checkQuestion: The area around the equator is hot all year, while the poles are freezing. Some children say 'the equator is hot because it's the part of Earth closest to the Sun.' Is that why? What really decides whether a place is in a hot, temperate, or polar climate zone?
checkAnswer: No — the equator isn't meaningfully closer to the Sun. Climate zone is decided mainly by latitude: near the equator the Sun's rays hit almost straight down and concentrate heat on a small area, while near the poles the same rays strike at a slant and spread over a larger area, so it's colder. Altitude and distance from the sea also matter.
